vtrmc-1979-01.title: Calculus in one variable
vtrmc-1979-01.body:
Let the radius be $r>0$ and the height $h>0$. The volume is fixed: $V=\pi r^2h$, so $h=\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}$. The total surface area (two discs plus the side) is
$$A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi r^2+\frac{2V}{r},\qquad r>0.$$
Then
$$A'(r)=4\pi r-\frac{2V}{r^2}=\frac{2(2\pi r^3-V)}{r^2}.$$
So $A'<0$ for $r^3<\frac{V}{2\pi}$ and $A'>0$ for $r^3>\frac{V}{2\pi}$: $A$ is strictly decreasing and then strictly increasing, and it has a unique global minimum at $r_0$ with $2\pi r_0^3=V$.

At this radius
$$h=\frac{V}{\pi r_0^2}=\frac{2\pi r_0^3}{\pi r_0^2}=2r_0,$$
so the altitude equals the diameter. Conversely, $h=2r$ means $V=2\pi r^3$, i.e. $r=r_0$. Hence the cylinder of least surface area is exactly the one whose diameter equals its altitude. ∎

vtrmc-1979-01.title: AM-GM
vtrmc-1979-01.body:
With $h=V/(\pi r^2)$ the area is $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{V}{r}+\dfrac{V}{r}$. By AM-GM for three positive numbers,
$$A\ge 3\sqrt[3]{2\pi r^2\cdot\frac{V}{r}\cdot\frac{V}{r}}=3\sqrt[3]{2\pi V^2},$$
a constant, with equality if and only if the three terms are equal: $2\pi r^2=\dfrac{V}{r}=\pi r h$, i.e. $h=2r$. So the minimum is attained exactly when the altitude equals the diameter. ∎

vtrmc-1979-02.title: Insert the identity cleverly
vtrmc-1979-02.body:
Both statements are true (this is the Eckmann–Hilton argument).

**(b) Commutativity.** For $a,b\in S$, using (i) and then (ii) with the four elements $e,a,b,e$:
$$a\circ b=(e\circ a)\circ(b\circ e)=(e\circ b)\circ(a\circ e)=b\circ a.$$

**(a) Associativity.** For $a,b,c\in S$, using (i) and (ii) with the four elements $a,b,e,c$:
$$(a\circ b)\circ c=(a\circ b)\circ(e\circ c)=(a\circ e)\circ(b\circ c)=a\circ(b\circ c).$$

So $\circ$ is both associative and commutative. ∎

vtrmc-1979-03.title: Similarity
vtrmc-1979-03.body:
**(a) True.** Since conjugation of entries respects products and sums, $\bar B=\overline{A\bar A+I}=\bar A A+I$. Now
$$A^{-1}BA=A^{-1}(A\bar A+I)A=A^{-1}A\bar AA+A^{-1}A=\bar AA+I=\bar B.$$

**(b) True.** By (a), $B$ and $\bar B$ are similar, so $\det\bar B=\det(A^{-1}BA)=\det(A)^{-1}\det B\det A=\det B$. On the other hand the determinant is a polynomial with integer coefficients in the entries, so $\det\bar B=\overline{\det B}$. Hence $\det B=\overline{\det B}$, i.e. $\det(A\bar A+I)$ is real. ∎

vtrmc-1979-03.title: Characteristic polynomials (part (b), even without nonsingularity)
vtrmc-1979-03.body:
For any square matrices $X,Y$ of the same size, $XY$ and $YX$ have the same characteristic polynomial; in particular $\det(XY+I)=\det(YX+I)$ (for invertible $X$ this is $YX+I=X^{-1}(XY+I)X$; in general it follows by continuity, since invertible matrices are dense).

Take $X=A$, $Y=\bar A$:
$$\det(A\bar A+I)=\det(\bar AA+I)=\det\big(\overline{A\bar A+I}\big)=\overline{\det(A\bar A+I)},$$
so the determinant equals its own conjugate and is real. ∎

vtrmc-1979-04.title: Mean value theorem
vtrmc-1979-04.body:
Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $f'(x)\to0$, there is $X>0$ such that $|f'(t)|<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge X$.

For $x>X$ the mean value theorem gives some $\xi\in(X,x)$ with $f(x)-f(X)=f'(\xi)(x-X)$, hence
$$|f(x)|\le |f(X)|+\varepsilon(x-X)\le |f(X)|+\varepsilon x.$$
Dividing by $x$,
$$\left|\frac{f(x)}{x}\right|\le\frac{|f(X)|}{x}+\varepsilon .$$
The first term tends to $0$ as $x\to\infty$ ($X$ is fixed), so there is $X'$ with $|f(x)/x|<2\varepsilon$ for all $x>X'$. As $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)/x=0$. ∎

vtrmc-1979-04.title: Integral form
vtrmc-1979-04.body:
Because $f'$ is continuous, $f(x)=f(X)+\int_X^x f'(t)\,dt$ for $x>X$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $X$ with $|f'(t)|<\varepsilon$ for $t\ge X$; then
$$\left|\frac{f(x)}{x}\right|\le\frac{|f(X)|}{x}+\frac1x\int_X^x|f'(t)|\,dt\le\frac{|f(X)|}{x}+\varepsilon\cdot\frac{x-X}{x}<\frac{|f(X)|}{x}+\varepsilon .$$
Letting $x\to\infty$ gives $\limsup_{x\to\infty}|f(x)/x|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so the limit is $0$. ∎

vtrmc-1979-05.title: Work modulo 2 and modulo 7
vtrmc-1979-05.body:
Let $N=3^{4n+2}+5^{2n+1}$.

* **Mod 2:** both powers are odd, so $N$ is even.
* **Mod 7:** $3^{4n+2}=9\cdot 81^n$ and $5^{2n+1}=5\cdot25^n$. Since $9\equiv2$, $81\equiv4$ and $25\equiv4\pmod 7$,
$$N\equiv 2\cdot4^n+5\cdot4^n=7\cdot4^n\equiv0\pmod 7.$$

As $\gcd(2,7)=1$, $14\mid N$ for every $n\ge1$ (in fact also for $n=0$, where $N=14$). ∎

vtrmc-1979-05.title: Induction
vtrmc-1979-05.body:
Let $N_n=3^{4n+2}+5^{2n+1}$. For $n=1$: $N_1=729+125=854=14\cdot61$.

Suppose $14\mid N_n$. Then
$$N_{n+1}=81\cdot3^{4n+2}+25\cdot5^{2n+1}=25N_n+56\cdot3^{4n+2}.$$
Both $25N_n$ and $56\cdot3^{4n+2}=14\cdot4\cdot3^{4n+2}$ are divisible by $14$, so $14\mid N_{n+1}$. By induction $14\mid N_n$ for all $n\ge1$. ∎

vtrmc-1979-06.title: Telescoping comparison
vtrmc-1979-06.body:
**It converges** (and the hypothesis that $\sum a_n$ diverges is not even needed).

Since all $a_n>0$, the partial sums increase: $0<S_{n-1}<S_n$ for $n\ge2$. Hence for $n\ge2$
$$\frac{a_n}{S_n^2}\le\frac{a_n}{S_{n-1}S_n}=\frac{S_n-S_{n-1}}{S_{n-1}S_n}=\frac1{S_{n-1}}-\frac1{S_n}.$$
Summing from $n=2$ to $N$ telescopes:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{a_n}{S_n^2}\le\frac{a_1}{S_1^2}+\frac1{S_1}-\frac1{S_N}<\frac{2}{a_1}.$$
The partial sums of the positive series are bounded, so $\sum a_n/S_n^2$ converges. (Since $S_N\to\infty$, the bound even shows the sum is at most $2/a_1$.) ∎

**Answer: the series converges.**

vtrmc-1979-06.title: Compare with an integral
vtrmc-1979-06.body:
For $n\ge2$ the function $1/t^2$ is decreasing, so on $[S_{n-1},S_n]$ (an interval of length $a_n$) it is at least $1/S_n^2$:
$$\frac{a_n}{S_n^2}\le\int_{S_{n-1}}^{S_n}\frac{dt}{t^2}.$$
Adding these for $n=2,\dots,N$,
$$\sum_{n=2}^N\frac{a_n}{S_n^2}\le\int_{S_1}^{S_N}\frac{dt}{t^2}\le\int_{a_1}^\infty\frac{dt}{t^2}=\frac1{a_1}.$$
Bounded partial sums of a positive series mean convergence.

**Answer: the series converges.**

vtrmc-1979-07.title: Structure of $S$, then counting
vtrmc-1979-07.body:
**(a)** $S=\{0,1,2,\dots,9\}$ works: for $x,y\in S$, $|x-y|$ is an integer between $0$ and $9$. (So does $\{0,d,2d,\dots,9d\}$ for any $d\ge1$.)

**(b) The statement is true**, where "two elements" may be the same element twice (this is necessary: $0=a-a$ is the only way to write $0$ as a difference).

*Step 1: the structure of $S$.* If $S=\varnothing$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $0=|x-x|\in S$. If $S=\{0\}$ the claim is $0=0-0$. Otherwise let $d$ be the least positive element and $m=\max S$.
* Every $s\in S$ is a multiple of $d$: if $s\ge d$ then $s-d=|s-d|\in S$; repeating, the remainder $r=s\bmod d$ lies in $S$ with $0\le r<d$, so $r=0$.
* Every multiple of $d$ up to $m$ is in $S$: $m-d\in S$, $m-2d=|(m-d)-d|\in S$, and so on down to $0$.

Hence $S=\{0,d,2d,\dots,kd\}$ with $k=m/d$. Dividing everything by $d$ (which preserves sums, differences and the hypothesis) we may assume $S=\{0,1,\dots,k\}$, with $N=k+1$ elements, and $|A|>\frac{2N}{3}$.

*Step 2: counting.* Fix $s\in S$ and suppose, for contradiction, that $s\ne a+b$ and $s\neq a-b$ for all $a,b\in A$. Consider the subsets of $S=\{0,\dots,k\}$
$$A,\qquad P=\{a+s:\ a\in A,\ a\le k-s\},\qquad Q=\{s-a:\ a\in A,\ a\le s\}.$$
* $A\cap P=\varnothing$: an element $a'=a+s$ of both would give $s=a'-a$.
* $A\cap Q=\varnothing$: an element $a'=s-a$ of both would give $s=a'+a$.
* $P\subseteq[s,k]$ and $Q\subseteq[0,s]$, so $P\cap Q\subseteq\{s\}$.

Therefore $|A|+|P|+|Q|-1\le|A\cup P\cup Q|\le k+1$.

Now $|P|=|A\cap[0,k-s]|\ge|A|-s$, because the interval $[k-s+1,k]$ contains only $s$ integers, and $|Q|=|A\cap[0,s]|\ge|A|-(k-s)$ for the same reason. Thus
$$3|A|-k-1\le|A|+|P|+|Q|-1\le k+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |A|\le\frac{2(k+1)}{3}=\frac{2N}{3},$$
contradicting $|A|>\frac{2N}3$. So every $s\in S$ is a sum or a difference of two elements of $A$. ∎

*Remark.* The bound is sharp: for $S=\{0,1,2\}$ and $A=\{0,2\}$ (exactly two-thirds), $1$ is neither a sum nor a difference of elements of $A$.

vtrmc-1979-08.title: Count monomials and bound by degree
vtrmc-1979-08.body:
Throughout, $d_n(S)$ is the dimension of the linear span of $\Omega_n(S)$.

**(a)** The products of at most two elements of $\{1,x,x+1,y\}$ include $1=1\cdot1$, $x$, $y$, $x^2=x\cdot x$, $xy$, $y^2$. Every product of at most two of these polynomials has total degree $\le2$, so it lies in the span of the six monomials $1,x,y,x^2,xy,y^2$; and all six monomials are themselves in $\Omega_2$. Hence the span is exactly the $6$-dimensional space of polynomials of degree $\le 2$, and
$$d_2(\{1,x,x+1,y\})=6.$$

**(b)** A product of $k\le n$ factors from $\{1,x,y\}$ is a monomial $x^iy^j$ with $i+j\le k\le n$. Conversely every monomial $x^iy^j$ with $i+j\le n$ occurs: take $i$ factors $x$, $j$ factors $y$ and (if $i+j<1$, or to fill up) factors $1$ — e.g. $x^iy^j\cdot 1$ uses $i+j+1\le n$ factors if $i+j<n$, and $i+j=n$ factors otherwise. Distinct monomials are linearly independent, so $d_n$ is the number of pairs $(i,j)$ of non-negative integers with $i+j\le n$:
$$d_n(\{1,x,y\})=\sum_{t=0}^n(t+1)=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}.$$

**(c)** *Upper bound.* Let $D\ge1$ be at least the maximum total degree of the polynomials in $S$. Every element of $\Omega_n(S)$ has degree $\le nD$, so
$$d_n(S)\le\dim\{\text{polynomials of degree}\le nD\}=\binom{nD+2}{2}\le (nD+2)^2\le (3Dn)^2 .$$
Hence $\dfrac{\log d_n(S)}{\log n}\le 2+\dfrac{2\log(3D)}{\log n}\to2$, so $\varlimsup\le 2$ for every $S$ (when $d_n(S)\ge1$; if $S=\{0\}$ or $S=\varnothing$ the expression is not even defined and can be ignored).

*The bound is attained.* For $S=\{1,x,y\}$, by (b) $\log d_n/\log n=\log\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2\big/\log n\to2$.

So the least upper bound is $\boxed{2}$ (and it is attained). ∎
